narrative.text: The cover page of the Arabic edition of a casebook on ethical issues in international health research, produced by WHO's research ethics review committee secretariat with the University of Geneva; the extracted text is partly garbled.
The title page of the Arabic casebook on ethical issues in international health research, naming its authors, co-editor and editorial advisers from the University of Geneva.

The cataloguing and copyright page of the Arabic casebook, translated by the WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean from the 2009 English edition. It gives subject headings, ISBNs, standard disclaimers and permission details.

The first page of the casebook's contents, listing chapter 1 on defining research, with cases such as SARS and airline passengers, and chapter 2 on study design. Cases cover vaccine trials, TB prevention in HIV, race as a risk factor and traditional medicine; the page numbers are garbled.

Continues the contents with more design cases and chapter 3 on harms and benefits, including vaccine trials and pregnancy in research. It then begins chapter 4 on voluntary informed consent, with cases such as high-dose vitamin A in children and breast cancer in South Asia.

Continues the contents with further consent cases, such as stem cell donations and research among the elderly, and chapter 5 on standard of care. It begins chapter 6 on obligations to participants and communities.

Continues the contents with cases on obligations to communities, such as malaria and cholera vaccine trials and research on war-affected health systems. It also lists chapter 7 on privacy and confidentiality, with cases including a nevirapine study in West Africa.

Ends the contents with further privacy cases and chapter 8 on professional ethics, covering cases on research misconduct, conflicting loyalties and credit for ideas, followed by suggested readings and an annex.

The acknowledgements explain that the casebook came from a research ethics training project between WHO and the University of Geneva funded by the Geneva International Academic Network. They thank the Geneva colleagues and the many contributors of case studies, including staff of Johns Hopkins University. The text is signed by the editors in March 2009.

The foreword states that ethical research is vital to WHO's work and that strong ethical standards must be understood and applied by researchers and sponsors, especially in low-resource settings. It presents case-based group discussion as an effective way to learn to apply ethical principles and is signed by WHO's Assistant Director-General for information, evidence and research.

Gives biographies of the editors, including Richard Cash of the Harvard School of Public Health, known for early oral rehydration trials in what is now Bangladesh, and Daniel Wikler, who works on ethics and population health. Other editors' roles in bioethics and international medical research organizations are also described.
A near-empty page with a short garbled string.

The introduction explains that the casebook contains 64 case studies, each raising a hard ethical issue in planning, reviewing or conducting health research, especially international studies. It is meant to aid teaching, from short workshops to degree courses, and includes a facilitator's guide. It notes growing international concern that health research can both benefit and harm the communities studied.

Notes that risk of harm is greater where participants are poor, illiterate or lack other access to care, and that all WHO-supported research is reviewed by WHO ethics committees. It explains that the committee secretariat has long used case studies in its training, with experts from the Harvard School of Public Health, and that the cases grew out of more than a decade of joint workshops.
A blank page with no extracted text.
A near-empty page with a short garbled string.

Opens the facilitator's guide, explaining that case-based teaching differs from lectures and requires skill in leading discussion. The guide covers both the process of teaching with cases and key issues in their content, with sample questions, and ends with terms for reusing the material.

Describes the facilitator's role in case-based discussion, shifting the focus from lecturer to participants who learn by applying knowledge and experience. It acknowledges that some teachers may feel facilitation falls short of their duty, but argues it needs more skill and knowledge than lecturing. It cites the Declaration of Helsinki among source materials.

Gives sample discussion questions about interpreting guidelines, research context and benefits to trial participants, and advises choosing cases that bring out differences in culture, discipline and interests while respecting local cultural, religious and sexual norms. It also discusses whether to present a case before or after background teaching.

Weighs starting with a case versus a lecture and advises on finding a good starting point for discussion. It suggests splitting large groups into small groups of six to eight for 20–30 minutes, with the facilitator moving between them. It also encourages challenging the reasoning of participants who share the facilitator's views.

Offers practical guidelines for facilitating group discussion, such as creating a safe, supportive setting, treating everyone equally, addressing the whole group and helping those speaking in a second language. It closes by noting that a good discussion can lead to unexpected insights, as in Socratic dialogue.

Opens the facilitator's guide to the chapters of the Arabic edition of the WHO Casebook on ethical issues in international health research. It explains that cases are grouped by their main ethical issue but can be regrouped, for example by reproductive health or region. It then poses discussion questions on what patients must know before becoming research participants, the purpose of informed consent and when enrolling patients may be wrong.

Continues the facilitator's questions on vulnerability, asking whether people with limited access to care or ethnic minorities should be treated as vulnerable and whether consent is truly voluntary when research is the only route to care. It then refers to the Declaration of Helsinki and CIOMS guidelines as background. The cited web addresses are partly garbled in the extraction.

Explains how a casebook chapter can explore the tension between research and medical care and the evolution of research ethics guidelines, and suggests using it to train research ethics committee members on their remit. It lists suggested readings, including works on deception in social psychology and WHO guidance on study design and consent in low-resource settings. Some URLs in the extracted text are garbled.

Discusses the facilitator notes on the relationship between scientific soundness and ethics, including whether ethics committees should judge scientific validity or refer it to experts. It recommends a companion casebook for background examples. It lists readings, including a study on using mystery clients to evaluate condom negotiations in Malawi.

Covers casebook discussion topics on whether placebo control arms are ethical and under what conditions, along with equipoise and randomization. It points to CIOMS guidelines, the Declaration of Helsinki and other texts on placebo use. References include a US National Bioethics Advisory Commission report on clinical trials in developing countries.

Describes facilitator notes on benefits to families, communities and countries, not only individuals, noting little consensus on how far such obligations extend. It asks participants to consider risks to participants during and after research, for example in studies of violence against women. It then introduces the question of how to ensure research information and consent are properly conveyed, warning against exporting a single consent format across countries.

Continues the discussion of informed consent, arguing that individual consent requirements can be exported but not a uniform consent format, and noting the ambiguity of the term itself. It suggests alternative terms that separate adequate disclosure from comprehension. It cites a study of oophorectomy and tamoxifen in Vietnamese and Chinese women relevant to one case.

Raises further consent questions, such as when signing forms is inappropriate, the special sensitivity of violence-against-women research, literacy and who may consent on behalf of minors or people lacking capacity. It then introduces the chapter on standard of care and the debate over a single universal standard in multinational trials, citing the Nuffield Council on Bioethics.

Poses questions on the standard of care in trials, such as whether providing the best care anywhere is an undue inducement, and what happens when it cannot be continued after the trial. It also asks whether offering only the local standard of care exploits vulnerable people. It points to two recent HIV prevention trial guidance documents as useful frameworks.

Cites UNAIDS/WHO guidance on ethical considerations and good participatory practice in HIV prevention trials. It then notes that obligations in health research is a broad topic and advises facilitators to examine specific issues systematically. Questions cover ancillary care and building research capacity, with a reference on researchers' ancillary-care responsibilities.

Introduces the casebook chapter on privacy and confidentiality, suggesting that facilitators start from the idea that the value placed on them varies across cultures. It raises questions on data protection, who holds legal access to data and for how long, when data may be destroyed and the security of electronic records, citing an article on public health and data protection.

Introduces the chapter on professional ethics, focusing on conflicts of interest and scientific misconduct. It notes faculty financial ties to industry and the incentives linked to commercially funded trials, such as rapid recruitment and ghost-writing. It lists resources for case-based teaching, including a case study on the Tuskegee syphilis study.
A list of further readings on case-based teaching, including Harvard Kennedy School and other online resources; the web addresses are garbled in the extracted text.
A blank page with no extracted text.
A section divider page titled "Case studies".
A blank page with no extracted text.
A blank page with no extracted text.

Introduces the casebook chapter on when ethics committee review is required, explaining that defining research matters both in principle and for deciding which activities need review. It explores how research differs from medical care, surveillance, programme evaluation and quality improvement. It notes that growing social and behavioural research and government surveys blur the line between research and other activities.

Stresses that the pursuit of knowledge must not override human welfare, recalling Nazi concentration camp experiments and other abuses in which scientific or political zeal caused serious harm. It describes how the Nuremberg trial of Nazi doctors in 1947 produced the Nuremberg Code. The Code made voluntary consent essential, along with minimizing harm and balancing benefits and risks.

Explains why independent research ethics committees were created after notorious unethical studies, and the various names they go by. It describes their remit over both participants and the research itself. It notes that activities such as operational research may carry hidden risks, for example by temporarily improving care in a study community.

Discusses how studies of new guidelines or treatment schedules may expose shortcomings and harm the careers of staff involved. It notes that research ethics committees may lack authority over non-research activities such as public health surveillance, despite their competing aims. It also covers the difficult line between audit and research, citing an article with illustrative cases.

A case study on SARS and airline passengers in a country called "X", where a national centre conducting routine surveillance during the 2003 outbreak traced contacts of possible cases on flights using passenger manifests. It raises whether such activity counts as research needing ethics review.

A case study on a family and youth institute evaluating donor-funded sexual health and family planning programmes, including adolescent HIV testing and counselling, in developing countries. Questions ask how research differs from programme evaluation, whether ethics oversight is needed and what low risk means.

A case study of a neurosurgeon in an Asian capital who has injected olfactory stem cells from aborted fetuses into hundreds of patients with conditions such as ALS, Parkinson's disease and paralysis, calling it innovative therapy and refusing a controlled trial. Questions ask whether this is treatment, experimentation or research and who should monitor doctors' activities.

A case study on a university team asked to document the health of an isolated indigenous community threatened by encroaching farmers and loggers, with funds to be spent within three months. The study combined household surveys with blood sampling, including for genetic markers. Questions address protections, genetic harms, benefits to the community and duties to a child who fell ill.
A blank page with no extracted text.
The title page of the casebook's chapter 2, on issues in study design.

Introduces the chapter on study design, asking whether ethics committees should assess the scientific adequacy of protocols and splitting this into whether scientific quality is an ethical concern and who should judge it. It argues that exposing participants to harm or inconvenience is only justified by expected benefits. It also identifies three tasks in reviewing design and considers which belong to ethics committees.

Argues that institutions with peer review expertise can provide separate scientific review, but where resources are limited, as in many developing countries, ethics committees may need to assess both science and ethics. It notes that a member who finds a major design flaw cannot in conscience approve it. References include the CIOMS guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki.

Discusses debates over placebo-controlled versus active-comparator trials, including sponsors' preference for placebos and ethical concerns where effective treatment is unavailable locally. It also asks whether testing drugs that will not be affordable in the host country is justified. It defines equipoise and contrasts a narrow view of the committee's role with broader ethical concerns about design.

Discusses protecting participants in natural experiments, such as studying non-immune highlanders who move to malaria-endemic lowlands, and whether investigators must prevent harm even if the study becomes impossible. It considers possible coercion when nurses or students are recruited. It also notes the historical exclusion of women and children from research.

Notes that excluding women and children has left little evidence on treatment safety for them. It discusses a second ethical issue in design, the purpose of research, arguing that controlled studies are preferable to adopting untested innovations. It cites UNAIDS/WHO guidance supporting the ethical inclusion of women and children in HIV prevention trials.

Explains that ethics committees must weigh participant burdens against social benefits, ensure fair selection and check understanding, and decide whether to consider wider issues such as relevance to local health needs. It cites an author who used a mystery client design without informed consent to provoke debate on such research.
Summarizes a BMJ article contrasting the uncertainty principle with clinical equipoise as the ethical basis for randomized controlled trials.

A case study in the Arabic research ethics casebook on a study in South-East Asia of how many seriously ill children reach hospital under the WHO/UNICEF Integrated Management of Childhood Illness strategy, noting that about ten million children under five die each year. Questions ask what help caregivers should receive to get children to hospital, especially if it cannot continue after the study.

A case study of a European anthropologist in West Africa who used deceptive participant observation, with research assistants posing as clients of sex workers in bars and discos, to learn how condom use is negotiated. Questions address the ethics of deception, the role of ethics committees and problems in returning results to participants.

A case study of a South Asian investigator who planned to send young men posing as villagers to drug sellers to record the diarrhoea treatments they recommend for a sick toddler. Questions ask whether the deception is justified, what to do if advice is dangerous and whether sellers should be debriefed afterwards.

A case study on a placebo-controlled trial of a new hepatitis B vaccine in children in a high-burden, low-income setting, explaining the disease burden and existing vaccine types. Questions ask whether a placebo is ethical when local children have no other access to vaccination, how the study could be improved and whether one or both parents must consent.

A case study based on research over a decade old on preventing TB in people with HIV, explaining TB infection and why HIV raises the risk of active disease. It describes a placebo-controlled trial of preventive regimens in Africa. Questions ask whether the placebo arm was ethical and whether the study should have been done in Africa given that the costlier regimen would be unaffordable there.

A case study on developing a malaria vaccine, noting the resurgence of malaria, about a million deaths a year mostly among African children, and factors such as drug resistance and civil unrest. It describes a double-blind, placebo-controlled village trial where teams obtain caregiver consent, vaccinate children and then leave. Deaths and illness are tracked afterwards.

Continues the malaria vaccine case, explaining that mortality is the endpoint so investigators cannot intervene in natural malaria transmission, though cheap measures could reduce deaths. Questions ask who is responsible for ensuring local ethics review and what options exist if the host country lacks oversight capacity.

A case study from a southern African country where clinic records show that people who identify as "coloured" have twice the rate of sexually transmitted infections as those who identify as "black". It recalls apartheid-era racial classification. Questions ask whether such politically defined categories can be used in research and how the protocol could be strengthened, with footnotes defining race and ethnicity.

A case study on trials of short-course zidovudine to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission, describing the long, costly 076 regimen of the mid-1990s and the decision to test a shorter, cheaper regimen against placebo in developing countries. It quotes the Declaration of Helsinki's conditions for when placebo or no treatment is acceptable.

Sets out critics' arguments that control groups in the short-course zidovudine trials should have received the 076 regimen rather than placebo, citing the Declaration of Helsinki and double standards. Questions ask whether local authorities' judgements on relevance matter and whether testing in high-income countries would avoid double standards.

A case study on testing Ayush-64, a patented four-herb Ayurvedic preparation, for malaria in South Asia without animal or preclinical toxicity studies, given concerns about chloroquine resistance. It describes the trial design comparing it with chloroquine and primaquine. Footnotes explain primaquine's role in preventing relapse.

Completes the Ayush-64 case with details on treatment failure, relapse definitions and 28-day follow-up without tracing dropouts. Questions ask what evidence is needed before testing a traditional remedy in humans, whether the study was ethical and what was owed to patients who left.

A case study on evaluating a popular traditional remedy made from the plant Centella asiatica for bloody diarrhoea in South Asia, which had never been formally studied. An investigator wanted to test it against standard antibiotic treatment for dysentery. Questions ask whether the ethics committee applied a double standard and how disagreements could be resolved.

A case study on a population twin study in a South-East Asian country with high rates of suicide, alcohol dependence and somatoform disorders, involving about 2 000 twin pairs and 1 000 singletons. Questions concern obligations to participants and follow-up for those with severely ill identical twins, with a footnote defining somatoform disorders.

A case study on an observational study by university researchers in East Asia of newborn care practices in a community with high neonatal mortality, in which field workers watched mothers of infants under three months. Questions ask when a field worker should intervene, how the study could be redesigned and whether others in the household needed to consent.

A case study of a field worker in the same newborn care study who was told not to intervene but faced a family's plea for help. Questions ask whether her duty to help outweighs her study obligations and how she could handle a flood of similar requests.
A blank page with no extracted text.

Introduces chapter 3 of the casebook on whether research benefits and harms are fairly distributed, noting that scientific needs may not match participants' best interests. It discusses justice in sharing benefits, early-phase trials that offer participants no benefit and the duty of ethics committees to ensure harms are small. It also stresses that participants must receive an honest account of risks and benefits.

Discusses the difficulty of comparing harms and benefits of different kinds, studies where net prospects for participants are negative, and dilemmas over stopping trials early when trends emerge. It also addresses the risk of stigmatizing communities. It lists suggested readings, beginning with a BMJ study on unjustified exclusion of older people from research.

Continues the suggested readings for the chapter on harm and benefit, including articles on age restrictions in trials, ethical concerns in microbicide research and whether research in poor countries exploits people unable to afford the results.

A case study on rotavirus vaccines, explaining that rotavirus causes diarrhoea in young children everywhere but most of its estimated 527 000 annual deaths occur in low-income countries. It describes a vaccine withdrawn after links to intussusception and a North American manufacturer's refusal to transfer technology to a developing-country firm.

Raises questions on whether a vaccine linked to intussusception should still be used where rotavirus kills many children, and who decides acceptable risk. It explains compulsory licensing under the TRIPS agreement as a way for governments to use patented inventions.

A case study on a European company's pneumococcal pneumonia vaccine trial in Africa, where 20 000 infants were randomized and the vaccine protected 90% of recipients, while some scientists argued controls should not be vaccinated afterwards. Questions ask whether withholding vaccine from the control group was justified.

A case study on a breast cancer trial in which a data and safety monitoring board recommended stopping early after a promising drug showed benefit, while investigators wanted to continue to statistical significance or five years. Questions weigh scientific rigour against ethical choices and the plight of control-group women who relapsed.

A case study on a North American NGO testing a vaginal microbicide to prevent HIV in women at high risk, including sex workers, at sites in four African countries and one South Asian country. Because the product lacked safety data for pregnancy, the protocol dealt with women who became pregnant. A footnote explains compulsory licensing under TRIPS.

A case study from the mid-1990s on quinacrine pellets as a non-surgical method of female sterilization, used in tens of thousands of women in many countries despite conflicting evidence on safety. It notes the importance of contraception in reducing maternal deaths. It describes how some defended continued use as ethically necessary.

Asks whether quinacrine use could be justified where maternal mortality is high even if it caused cancer, whether unregistered drugs should be exported to developing countries and whether the researchers' conduct amounted to misconduct.
A blank page with no extracted text.
The title page of chapter 4 of the casebook, on voluntary informed consent.

Introduces chapter 4 on whether consent to research is voluntary, informed and competent, tracing informed consent from the Nuremberg Code to the Declaration of Helsinki and CIOMS guidelines. It notes how these texts have shaped research ethics and the difficulty of applying them in diverse settings. Some web addresses in the references are garbled in the extraction.

Discusses competence to consent, distinguishing legal capacity from the ability to understand unfamiliar research concepts, especially where research is uncommon. It also covers voluntariness and undue inducement, and the options open to ethics committees when consent may not be fully voluntary.

Lists what investigators should disclose for consent, such as risks and benefits, the study purpose, sponsors, conflicts of interest and compensation for injury, in written or oral form. It stresses that information alone does not ensure understanding. It cites CIOMS guidelines and a study of comprehension in a South African HIV vaccine trial.

Explains that consent shifts some responsibility to participants and that ethics committees must check arrangements for compensating harm. It then discusses dilemmas in applying the Nuremberg Code's consent rule today, including deception such as research assistants posing as customers of drug sellers.

A page from the Arabic edition of WHO's casebook on ethical issues in international health research, discussing whether studies that deceive drug sellers are acceptable if participants are debriefed afterwards, citing CIOMS guidance. It also questions whether one standard of informed consent should apply to all research, including minimal-risk studies, and stresses community consultation from the planning stage.

Describes informed consent as a process involving community meetings, time to consult family and possible re-consent at follow-up visits, rather than just a signed form. It then gives annotated readings on informed consent, including one on the 'therapeutic misconception'.

Further annotated readings on informed consent, including an article on legal versus ethical grounds for consent in HIV vaccine trials and a reference to community leaders consenting on behalf of eligible individuals.
An annotated reading on community engagement and individual informed consent in the International HapMap genetic variation project, which the authors describe as a positive experience.

Presents a case on a double-blind trial of periodic high-dose vitamin A for children aged 6 months to 5 years in a rural West African community governed by a traditional chief and elders, followed by discussion questions. The questions ask whether individual consent is always needed and how the field team and donor should have handled the consent problem.

Presents a case on a trial in a South Asian country of oophorectomy plus tamoxifen as adjuvant treatment for premenopausal women with breast cancer, which researchers said could not be run in the United States where adjuvant therapy is standard. It describes the proposed consent process, which did not disclose randomisation, and explains the procedures involved.

Concludes the breast cancer case by noting that those consulted found the consent approach acceptable, then asks whether differences between countries justify different consent practices and whether such a trial is justified in a low-resource setting.

Introduces a case on testing a vaginal microbicide to give women a self-controlled way to prevent HIV and other sexually transmitted infections, describing the qualities of an ideal microbicide. It notes that no effective microbicide against HIV yet exists.

Continues the microbicide case, describing HIV counselling, referral of women found to be infected and their option not to learn their results. It asks whether withholding HIV test results from participants was ethical even with their agreement.

Presents a case on a randomised study at an East Asian cancer hospital of radiotherapy after surgery for oesophageal cancer, conducted without ethics review and with patients not told they were in a trial. It describes the controversy when the results were published with a critical editorial, and asks whether scientific value justifies publishing ethically flawed research.

Presents a case on a cluster-randomised trial of vitamin A or beta-carotene supplements for pregnant women in South Asia, where maternal vitamin A deficiency is linked to poor birth outcomes. It describes the consent process used and defines some technical terms in footnotes.

Discussion questions for the maternal supplementation case, on the ethics of randomising communities rather than individuals, the adequacy of consent and whether participants needed to understand randomisation.

Presents a 1990s case on a study in Central Africa of HIV transmission through breastfeeding by HIV-positive mothers, which could change the ministry's advice to breastfeed regardless of HIV status. It describes how couples were enrolled and counselled and a conflict when spouses disagreed about breastfeeding.

Discussion questions for the breastfeeding case, on disclosing a woman's HIV status to her partner, the husband's role in feeding decisions, whether free care was an undue inducement and the investigator's role when spouses disagree.

Presents a case in which South American researchers used humanised mice injected with blood donated by a woman to study dengue vaccine candidates, and the woman later made requests about her anonymised samples. Questions ask whether she was properly informed about the research.

Presents a case on embryo donation for stem cell research in an unnamed country, where clinicians providing assisted reproduction obtained combined consent for treatment and donation of 'spare' embryos. Questions ask about using embryos for research unrelated to reproduction and about consent for future unspecified studies.

Presents a case on research into the health care needs of elderly people in a formerly nomadic community in the northern Sahara who often reached hospital with preventable conditions, raising questions of consent and community involvement. It ends with questions on how an ethics committee should review the survey.
A near-blank divider page whose extracted text is a few garbled characters.

Introduces the chapter on standards of care, which focuses on what care the control group of a randomised controlled trial should receive in developing countries, ranging from a single universal standard to a more context-based view. It cites the Declaration of Helsinki.

Discusses the universal-standard view, under which control groups must receive the best proven treatment, and its drawbacks, such as ruling out placebo-controlled trials of cheaper alternatives. It then turns to the local-standard view and how it may let researchers exploit settings where people lack treatment.

Sets out objections to the local standard of care, arguing that it lets sponsors exploit existing injustices and seek sites where they must provide little. It begins annotated readings on double standards in research in poor countries.
Annotated readings on standards of care, including an article on controversial paragraphs of the Declaration of Helsinki and the US Food and Drug Administration's plan to drop references to it.

Presents a 1990s case on a Phase III HIV vaccine trial planned by a Northern European company among injecting drug users in South-East Asia, focusing on what treatment should be provided to participants who become infected. It describes disagreements over providing antiretroviral therapy that was unavailable locally.

Concludes the HIV vaccine case with the researchers' argument that providing advanced care could be an undue inducement, then asks whether the study was ethical, what compromise might work and whether the company's gifts of equipment were appropriate.

Presents a case on a trial in a southern African country of a single-dose antiretroviral regimen to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission, whose results led WHO to deem further trials unethical. It raises issues about the trial's standards and refers to ICH good clinical practice guidelines.

Presents a case on research into quinacrine pellets for non-surgical female sterilisation, driven by the lack of access to surgical sterilisation in developing countries. It describes the method and its trials and defines technical terms in footnotes.

Describes how a published article triggered a backlash that halted quinacrine production, suspended trials and led some countries to criminalise its sale. Questions ask whether a 'double standard' can ever be appropriate and who should decide.

Presents a case on a multi-site randomised trial of vaginal microbicides in East African family planning clinics, where drugs are unaffordable and Pap smears are unavailable. It raises the question of what care trial participants should receive and explains what microbicides are.
A page with no extracted text.
A divider page for the chapter on obligations to participants and communities, with some garbled characters.

Introduces the chapter on the obligations of researchers and sponsors, describing health research as a partnership whose expectations should be clear from the start, especially where health care is scarce. It lists the types of health needs that may arise, such as access to a proven intervention after a trial and conditions unrelated to the research.

Continues listing health needs that may arise in research, with examples such as paediatricians running an epidemiological study being asked to treat sick local children, and the needs of participants' families and communities.

Discusses what sponsors owe when researchers feel a professional duty to provide care, and whether sponsors' expected profits create obligations. It then gives annotated readings, including one on commercially viable products derived from human tissue samples.
Annotated readings on researchers' duties of ancillary care, returning results to participants and community-linked research on cervical cancer in South Africa.
Further annotated readings, including a paper proposing a structured approach to care and treatment obligations in vaccine trials and a statement on continued access to interventions after a trial.

Presents a case based on a 1970s observational study of cervical cancer, noting the global death toll, the role of Pap smear screening and the grading of cervical dysplasia into low and high grade lesions.

From the Arabic edition of WHO's casebook on ethical issues in international health research, this page ends a case in which women with cervical dysplasia were followed without treatment until cancer developed, continuing even after published evidence showed dysplasia is a precursor of cancer. It closes with discussion questions, including whether the study was acceptable and how others could learn of its results.

An Arabic-language case in which a multinational company and East African scientists plan a placebo-controlled trial of a new malaria vaccine in children under five. It describes the setting, the study design and community and ethics committee concerns, including reliance on health centre staff for informed consent, and notes the local malaria species.

Concludes the malaria vaccine case: local representatives ask for free vaccination of all children for five years if the vaccine works, which the company rejects as unaffordable. Discussion questions ask about the ethical issues, consent procedures, treatment for participants who get malaria and the company's obligations to the wider population.

An Arabic-language case about a European university clinic assessing mental health problems among refugees and torture survivors, noting that mental health services for refugees are fragmented. It describes the study plan and the ethical difficulty that questioning participants about traumatic events could cause distress.

Discussion questions for the refugee mental health case, asking whether an ethics committee member should approve the protocol, about its risk–benefit balance and about informing participants of results under CIOMS guidance, and whether researchers must improve the care available to participants.

An Arabic-language case on a longitudinal study of rotavirus infection among young children in a deprived area of a West African city, where diarrhoeal disease is a leading cause of child death. It describes the study design, including free medical care and transport money for participants, and plans to report findings to the ministry of health.

Discussion questions on the rotavirus study, asking how free care and transport payments might influence mothers' enrolment and study results, and whether researchers had obligations to continue services or follow up with the ministry.

An Arabic-language case on a trial of a childhood cholera vaccine in an endemic area of South-East Asia, giving background on cholera, rehydration treatment and its costs. The page also includes background on related preventive measures, such as tetanus toxoid in pregnancy and clean delivery.

An Arabic-language case on a study by ministry of health researchers in a sub-Saharan African country of how armed conflict affects the health system and malaria control, collecting data from internally displaced people and host communities. Questions ask whether it was ethical to group displaced people and host community members together.

An Arabic-language case set in a South Asian farming district with a large, poor tribal population, describing how community representatives were chosen for a research project. It recounts concerns raised by young field workers that tribal views were excluded, which the principal investigator dismissed as the selection followed an accepted protocol.

Discussion questions on defining the community, asking whether participant selection was flawed, who represents a culturally diverse community, how minority views should be included and what obligations funders had; the case is credited to a Mumbai ethics centre (2007).

An Arabic-language case on evaluation research into disability rehabilitation programmes in a South Asian country, where a right-to-education law covered disabled children and funds were given to voluntary organizations for community-based services. It sets out the evaluation design and ethical questions for researchers and care providers, and credits a Mumbai ethics centre.

An Arabic-language case on a large randomized trial of an immune-modulating drug for people with HIV, run by North American academics and funded by a company that owned the data but agreed not to restrict publication. When results showed no benefit and the sponsor objected to publication, questions ask what the investigators could or should do.

An Arabic-language case on genetic research among a genetically homogeneous island population of about 90 000 under a monarchy with limited democracy. A company's plan to collect samples drew objections on grounds of values and religion, and the company withdrew to seek agreements elsewhere.

Discussion questions on the island genetic research case, about collective ownership of genetic heritage, governments' capacity to negotiate research agreements, benefit-sharing and whether a non-profit sponsor would change the ethics.
A blank page with no extractable text.

Introduces Chapter 7 of the Arabic casebook, on privacy and confidentiality, explaining that health research can threaten individuals' privacy and professionals' duty of confidentiality and that ethics committees must weigh risks when these conflict with science. It gives examples of harms from disclosure, such as revealing misattributed paternity through genetic testing.

Continues the Chapter 7 introduction with further examples of harm, such as job or insurance discrimination after disclosure of a Huntington disease gene, and notes that privacy matters even without tangible interests at stake. It discusses public health and electronic medical records as growing sources of controversy over confidentiality.

Discusses how genetic databases, electronic records and easy linkage of datasets threaten individuals' control over their health information, while also offering benefits for research. It warns investigators and ethics committees to take precautions against re-identification.

A list of suggested readings for the privacy and confidentiality chapter, with brief descriptions, including articles on disclosing individual research results and on public health and data protection; some web addresses are garbled in the extraction.

An Arabic-language case on a West African study of nevirapine given to HIV-positive pregnant women and their newborns to reduce perinatal transmission, in which women were promised confidentiality of their test results. Questions concern disclosure of HIV status and whether researchers should discuss a safety plan with women about sharing it.

An Arabic-language case on evaluating the quality of care in a family welfare programme in a South Asian state, funded through a European university grant and involving interviews and observation at primary health centres and a sterilization camp. It raises questions about protecting identities and is noted to be closely similar to another case in the book.

An Arabic-language case in which researchers guaranteed confidentiality to primary health centres and staff in a South Asian family welfare evaluation, but faced challenges when presenting their findings to officials. Questions ask when, if ever, promises of confidentiality may be overridden.

An Arabic-language case on a study of complications after abortion in an Eastern European country where legal abortion is hard to access and illegal abortions remain common. It describes recruitment through women's homes and interviewing techniques to create privacy, such as decoy interviews with other family members.

Continues the abortion complications case: an anthropologist on the funder's ethics committee worried that participants' identities could be exposed, and the investigator replied that records would be locked away at the NGO's head office. Questions ask whether the recruitment method was appropriate and free of coercion.

An Arabic-language case on a Central American mental health institute's research to check whether community mental health centres deliver the services they are paid for, using patient records. Questions ask whether valid consent was needed and what an ethics committee should advise.

An Arabic-language case in which molecular biologists plan to study genetic links between brain-wave patterns and alcoholism in North American Indigenous tribes, raising concerns about research on identifiable populations. It asks how the protocol could address these concerns and credits a case from the US National Human Genome Research Institute.

An Arabic-language case on a proposed telephone-based case–control study of vasectomy and prostate cancer, with controls drawn from electoral rolls. The ethical question concerns whether revealing the study's purpose would bias answers.

An Arabic-language case in which social scientists, given access to hospital records, visited women who had not returned for abnormal Pap smear results in order to understand and improve services. It raises privacy concerns and notes the value of cervical screening.

An Arabic-language case on health promotion research at a large commercial farm in southern Africa employing seasonal workers, many of them young unmarried women. Researchers found underage girls working there, apparently at risk of sexual exploitation, and were unsure how to respond.

Discussion questions on the farm case, asking whether researchers should have told farm management about the underage girls and their risk of sexually transmitted infections including HIV, and what obligations researchers had.

An Arabic-language case on interviewing child domestic servants in sub-Saharan Africa, describing how the traditional practice of child fostering is increasingly exploited to recruit and traffic young girls for domestic work. It considers the precautions the researchers took and asks whether they would be needed with adult servants.
A blank page with no extractable text.
A near-blank page whose extracted text consists of only a few stray characters.

Introduces Chapter 8 of the Arabic casebook, on professional ethics, asking what to do when loyalties are divided and how research misconduct should be defined and handled. It sets out expectations of integrity, such as no fabrication, falsification or plagiarism, accurate authorship and disclosure of conflicts of interest. It begins discussing conflicts of interest and why they have become important in health research.

Explains that the growth of industry-funded research and scientists' financial ties to companies have made conflicts of interest a major concern in health research. It discusses how such conflicts can affect research and how they are managed, citing CIOMS guidance.

Discusses how conflicts of interest can threaten participants who rely on research for care and may not understand disclosures, calling for evidence-based policies and noting that ethics committee members can also have conflicts. It then turns to research misconduct and cites suggested readings.

Discusses whether research misconduct should be judged the same way across countries and cultures, arguing that core issues such as falsifying data are universal even if laboratory practices once differed. It ends with notes and a reference.

Suggested readings for a chapter of the Arabic edition of WHO's casebook on ethical issues in international health research, with annotated entries on conflicts of interest in clinical drug trials and financial ties between review board members and industry. A further entry concerns conducting well-designed research ethically across cultures; some URLs are garbled OCR.

A case study in which a manufacturer of a new hormonal contraceptive commissions a trial comparing pills, patches and injections among women of different educational levels, paying salaries and providing computers to regional researchers. It ends with discussion questions and a source note citing a seminar of the WHO-hosted human reproduction research programme in Bangkok.

A case study in which an Asian drug company, told to do more testing after heart rhythm problems appeared, contracts a crowded long-stay psychiatric hospital in eastern Europe to test a new antipsychotic for schizophrenia. It describes the vulnerable patients, many without close relatives, and includes background on schizophrenia.

A case study in which a North American university proposes a large family planning study to a medical school ethics committee in South-East Asia but wants its budget reviewed separately from the scientific and ethical review. It raises questions about whether ethics committees should review budgets and overhead charges.

A case study in which an employee benefits group at a West African mining company asks a European university team to estimate the cost of AIDS to its workforce, hoping to prompt prevention programmes. The findings include rising health-care costs that could reach a large share of operating costs. The case then begins to describe legal obligations for treating diagnosed employees.

Continues the mining company case, in which the report's recommendations alarm managers and the chief executive warns that paying for HIV care could bankrupt the company or force it to relocate. Questions ask what the research team should have done and whether the company should shape the report's recommendations.

A case study in which a community NGO in a South Asian city partners with researchers to study the effects of resettling slum residents, but tensions arise as the research design sidelines the NGO staff's experience. The NGO comes to feel the study is not meeting its goal of supporting an advocacy campaign. The case touches on involving just one NGO worker to maintain separation from the research team.

Discussion questions for the resettlement case on the ethics committee's decision, community expectations of direct help, informed consent and tensions between action and research, with a source note crediting a Mumbai ethics centre.

A case study in which a young research assistant finds that data from a respected senior researcher do not support the lab's theory linking blood lipids to age-related cardiovascular risk. After he returns a 'corrected' dataset that fits the theory, she notices entries were changed and he dismisses her concerns. The case follows her reporting of the problem and ends with the researcher's mitigating claims, such as his community science teaching, before sentencing.

Discussion questions on the data falsification case, about the researcher's justifications, whether the whistle-blower should be rewarded or punished, and the role of ethics committees in upholding research integrity.

A case study in which graduate students in a university genetics department conclude that their professor is fabricating data, for instance presenting previously published results as new in a grant application. When confronted she blames a computer error, which convinces some students but not others. The case describes the risks the students face and ends with questions on their options, the university's duties and treatment of whistle-blowers.

A case study about Dr Taylor, a renowned nutrition and immunology expert at a North American university, who ran an industry-sponsored study of whether a new infant formula could prevent allergy. A research nurse struggled to recruit 288 infants from allergy-prone families in a small city with a low birth rate. The case moves to a later study submitted to a journal, where reviewers doubted its validity and the author claimed the university had lost his data.

Continues the Taylor case, in which the journal rejects the study and asks the university to investigate, while another journal publishes it to wide acclaim. Two professors then uncover glaring errors that made the reported testing nearly impossible. Discussion questions address pressure on staff, professional bodies and journals' duty to review past articles.

A case study in which a prolific Central American researcher, after returning home, is asked by a funder to review a proposal from another prominent researcher that closely resembles a protocol he co-wrote earlier. It explores plagiarism and ownership of research ideas. Questions ask whether the funder applied different standards because he came from a developing country.

Further discussion questions on the plagiarism case, asking which ethical standards should apply and presenting scenarios about whether a research idea belongs to its originator and how authorship credit should be given.

Opens the casebook's glossary, defining terms such as adjuvant therapy, adenocarcinoma, adverse event and adverse drug reaction. A note says definitions come mainly from WHO publications and cites CIOMS ethical guidelines.
Continues the glossary with terms including anonymization, anthropometry, arrhythmia, audit in clinical trials and Ayurveda, with sources such as the ICH good clinical practice guidelines.

Continues the glossary with terms such as cancer, which it says caused 7.6 million of 58 million deaths in one year, and carcinoma in situ. It cross-references case-control studies to the research design entry. It also begins describing the CIOMS international ethical guidelines for biomedical research involving human subjects.

Continues the glossary, describing the purpose of the CIOMS guidelines for low-resource settings and the CIOMS guidelines for epidemiological studies. It also defines community and other terms, citing the 2008 Declaration of Helsinki.

Continues the glossary with definitions of effectiveness, efficacy, endpoint, epidemiology and equity, among others, citing sources such as a dictionary of epidemiology and a module on focus group discussions.

Continues the glossary with terms such as gonorrhoea, described as a sexually transmitted infection that may be symptomless. It defines good clinical practice as an ethical and scientific standard for trials stemming from the ICH guidelines. It explains that compliance assures participant protection consistent with the Declaration of Helsinki and credible trial data.
Continues the glossary with definitions of immunity, immunogenic, innovative therapy and related terms, citing ICH good clinical practice guidelines.

Continues the glossary with justice as fair distribution of the burdens and benefits of research and knowledge-attitude-practice surveys. It gives a detailed entry on malaria, covering transmission by mosquitoes, symptoms and drug resistance. It also cites the published record of the Nuremberg trials.
Continues the glossary with the Nuremberg Code, observational study, oophorectomy and oral rehydration therapy. It then begins describing the phases of clinical trials.
Completes the description of clinical trial phases II to IV and adds further terms, citing WHO malaria treatment guidelines.

Continues the glossary with a description of quinacrine used for non-surgical sterilization by groups other than WHO, noting insufficient efficacy data and high failure rates. It adds further terms, citing ICH good clinical practice guidelines.
Continues the glossary with terms such as deceptive research and double-blind study, explaining why blinding is used and when it is broken for safety. CIOMS guidelines are cited.

Continues the glossary with SARS, citing 8,089 cases in 26 countries by July 2003 and its strain on health services and travel. It defines schizophrenia and its treatability and sclerosing agents, among other terms. Sources include the US National Cancer Institute and American Cancer Society guidelines.
Continues the glossary with standard operating procedures, stem cells, stigma and structured interviews, citing sources such as the US National Institutes of Health.
Ends the glossary with terms such as compulsory licensing, tubal ligation, tuberculosis and whistle-blowing.

Introduces the casebook's suggested readings and resources, organized by ethics guidelines, ethics review committees, international health research ethics and readings for each chapter. It lists the chapter topics and ends with online training resources, including a bilingual distance-learning initiative on research ethics review for Africa.

Part of the suggested readings in the Arabic research ethics casebook, describing UNESCO's bioethics work and its Global Ethics Observatory databases. It also annotates the ICH good clinical practice guideline, which sets unified standards for the EU, Japan and the US. Some web addresses are garbled in the extraction.

Continues the annotated readings with the US National Bioethics Advisory Commission report on clinical trials in developing countries and the UNAIDS/WHO guidance on ethical considerations in HIV prevention trials, which sets out 19 guidance points.

Continues the annotated readings with UNAIDS guidance on good participatory practice in HIV prevention trials and WHO guidelines on good clinical practice for trials of pharmaceutical products, which aim to protect participants and ensure sound science.

Continues the annotated readings with the WHO handbook on good clinical research practice and the World Medical Association's Declaration of Helsinki, described as a statement of ethical principles for medical research on humans.

Continues the annotated readings with notes on the Declaration of Helsinki's revisions, the WTO TRIPS agreement on intellectual property and an overview of research ethics capacity-building initiatives in developing countries.

Continues the annotated readings with a case study of research ethics committees in Africa and an article on how political context and human rights conditions, such as risks to refugees, should shape where research is done.

Continues the annotated readings with an article proposing benchmarks for ethical clinical research in developing countries to avoid exploitation, and one arguing that North–South research partnerships should share burdens and benefits fairly.

Begins the chapter-by-chapter suggested readings, starting with CDC guidelines on distinguishing public health research from practice. It annotates further readings on defining research and on ethical challenges in multinational studies in low-resource settings.

Lists readings for the study design chapter, including an article on mystery clients in condom negotiation research in Malawi and guidance on ethically collecting information from children and adolescents.

Lists readings on consent, including an article on exporting tissue samples from developing countries and the need to engage communities, and one comparing legal and ethical grounds for informed consent in vaccine trials.

Lists readings including a WHO/TDR review of ethical challenges in study design and consent in low-resource settings, and an article on community consultation and individual consent in human genetic variation research.

Lists readings for the standard of care chapter, including an article arguing that requiring the best global standard of care can undermine useful research, and an article on researchers' ancillary-care responsibilities.

Lists further readings on obligations to participants, including a framework for ancillary care, a BMJ article on giving participants summaries of results, and a paper on locally relevant research using a cervical cancer initiative in South Africa.

Lists readings on obligations in vaccine trials and on professional ethics, including an article noting that conflicts of interest are common in industry-funded drug trials and may raise the risk of misconduct.

Lists readings on professional ethics, including a survey finding frequent financial ties between institutional review board members and industry and an article on reaching international consensus on scientific misconduct.

Introduces the ethical principles reprinted in the casebook from the CIOMS/WHO international guidelines for biomedical research, setting out respect for persons, beneficence and justice. It notes that other frameworks also exist. It stresses that research in low-resource settings should meet local health needs and make resulting products reasonably available.

Continues the CIOMS principle of justice, stating that research with vulnerable people must respond to their needs and that risks without prospect of direct benefit must be justified by benefits to the group represented.

The back cover of the Arabic casebook, noting that it came from a project of the WHO research ethics review committee secretariat with the University of Geneva and the Geneva International Academic Network.
